prompt_free_text:
This paper studies a simple but important mismatch in neural theorem proving: models are typically trained only on successful proof trajectories, yet at inference time they operate inside a search process that repeatedly proposes tactics, observes failures, and backtracks. The paper proposes to train on trial-and-error traces that include failed branches and backtracking, and evaluates this idea on a newly constructed Lean dataset for intuitionistic propositional logic, PropL. The central empirical claim is that a model trained with such traces, TrialMaster, achieves higher success and lower search cost than a conventional model trained only on successful paths and used within DFS. The paper is clearly motivated, the core intuition is sensible, and the experimental results suggest that failure-aware training can indeed help in this restricted proving domain.

I found the paper interesting and potentially valuable, especially because it isolates a concrete issue in theorem-proving pipelines and tests it in a controlled formal setting. The decision to work in intuitionistic propositional logic is reasonable for a first study: proofs are formally checkable, theorem generation can be systematic, and one can obtain complete search traces from a known proof procedure. The resulting setup allows the authors to ask a clean scientific question that is difficult to study on existing theorem-proving corpora. This is a real strength. The paper also makes a useful dataset contribution by constructing theorem/proof pairs with trial-and-error information, which is uncommon in current public resources.

The main positive aspect is the conceptual framing. The train-test discrepancy identified here is real: if a prover is deployed as a search agent, then failed actions are part of the inference-time experience, and ignoring them during training is suboptimal. The paper’s proposed remedy is straightforward and plausible. I also appreciate that the authors do not merely append error messages from Lean, but instead train on full search histories including backtracking structure. This is a distinct angle from some prior work. The ablation comparing TrialMaster to a model trained without trial-and-error but run under the same one-step inference protocol is particularly important; it helps separate the effect of the training data from the effect of the search algorithm.

That said, the paper currently has several methodological and presentation weaknesses that limit how strongly I can trust the conclusions and how broadly I can interpret them.

The biggest issue is that the comparison between TrialMaster and the DFS baseline is not fully controlled. TrialMaster and DFS differ along multiple axes simultaneously: training data, inference protocol, decoding strategy, and search mechanism. TrialMaster uses greedy one-step generation conditioned on the entire proof history and can emit explicit backtrack instructions; the DFS baseline samples multiple tactics per state with varying temperatures and relies on an external DFS controller. Because these systems are structurally different, the headline comparison does not isolate whether the gains come from learning from failures, from the particular prompting/history format, from explicit backtrack tokens, or from avoiding stochastic multi-sample decoding. The ablation in Table 3 partially addresses this by comparing two models under the same inference style, and in my view that ablation is actually the strongest evidence in the paper. However, the paper should foreground this more clearly and be more careful not to over-attribute all gains in the main comparison to trial-and-error training alone.

Relatedly, the baseline space is too narrow. The paper compares primarily against a proof-only model inside DFS, but there are several more informative controls that are missing. For example, one could train on successful proofs augmented with the same full history format but without failed branches, to test whether the benefit comes from richer sequential context rather than failure supervision. One could also compare against a model trained on trial-and-error traces but disallowed from outputting backtrack instructions, to disentangle “learning from failures” from “learning an explicit control language.” Another useful baseline would be a proof-only model run greedily in the same autoregressive history-conditioned setting as TrialMaster, beyond the single ablation table, with more detailed metrics such as error types and average proof length. Without these controls, the causal interpretation remains somewhat underspecified.

A second major concern is the scope and external validity of the results. The entire study is conducted on synthetic intuitionistic propositional logic theorems of fixed formula size, with proofs generated by a deterministic or lightly randomized focused proof search procedure. This is a very constrained domain. It is useful scientifically, but the paper occasionally overstates the implications for “Automated Theorem Proving” more broadly. In this setting, the theorem distribution, proof language, and search dynamics are all heavily engineered. The model may be learning regularities of the FPS-generated traces as much as general principles of failure-aware proving. Since both training and evaluation proofs are produced by the same underlying proof-search formalism, there is a risk of procedural overfitting. The OOD split is based on proof length quantiles, which is a reasonable hardness split, but it is not a distribution shift in proof style or theorem family. I would encourage the authors to moderate claims and explicitly frame the work as evidence in a controlled domain rather than as a broadly established theorem-proving advance.

The dataset construction also raises some questions. The paper repeatedly claims that uniform sampling of integers combined with a bijection to formulas yields a “representative” sample of propositional logic theorems. This is too strong as stated. A bijection gives a way to enumerate formulas, but representativeness depends on the induced distribution over semantic and syntactic properties, not merely on existence of a bijection. Uniformity over integers up to some range does not necessarily correspond to a meaningful or balanced distribution over theorem difficulty, connective patterns, variable reuse, provability rate, or proof structure. Moreover, the paper fixes theorem statements to have 16 internal nodes, which further narrows the distribution. The authors should be much more precise here and avoid equating enumerability with representativeness.

There is also an incompleteness introduced in the proof generator: once an implication is picked, it cannot be used to show its premise. The paper says this affects only about 1 in 1000 randomly sampled provable theorems. This may be acceptable pragmatically, but it matters because the generated traces define the supervision signal and the proving environment. If the search procedure is incomplete and biased toward certain proof patterns, then the learned model may inherit those biases. At minimum, the paper should quantify how many training and test examples are impacted, whether any are excluded, and whether this restriction changes theorem/proof statistics in a measurable way.

The evaluation metrics are sensible but incomplete. Success rate and number of Lean calls are useful, especially since Lean calls proxy search cost. However, the paper does not report variance across runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Given that fine-tuning and decoding can be somewhat unstable, especially with small batch sizes and one epoch, it would be important to know whether the reported differences are robust across random seeds. This is particularly relevant for the OOD results, where differences among systems are not enormous in absolute terms except for the ablation. Similarly, the paper should report average and median proof lengths, average number of backtracks, Lean syntax error rates, and failure mode breakdowns. The claim that TrialMaster “learns backtracking capability” is currently supported only by the observation that backtrack instructions are well-formed and refer to existing states. That is not enough. The more important question is whether those backtracks are semantically useful and improve eventual success relative to not backtracking.

Another issue is fairness of the stopping criteria. TrialMaster fails immediately upon any Lean error, whereas DFS can continue exploring alternatives after invalid tactics at a state. This seems to disadvantage TrialMaster, and the authors mention that the 1500-word limit is also stricter for their method. That is good to acknowledge. But the converse is that TrialMaster can emit backtrack instructions without incurring Lean calls, while DFS pays for each checked tactic. Since the systems are architecturally different, search-cost comparisons should be interpreted carefully. It would help to report additional normalized metrics, such as success versus wall-clock time, success versus model tokens generated, or success under a fixed total inference budget including both model generation and Lean checking. Right now, the cost metric favors the framing of the proposed method but does not capture total computational expense.

The paper’s presentation of results is also somewhat incomplete because the key OOD figure is referenced but not actually visible in the provided text. Since the main claim rests on OOD superiority, the paper should ensure that exact numerical results are clearly tabulated, not only plotted. Table 3 gives one important ablation number, but the full comparison against DFS across hyperparameters should be available in a table in the main paper or appendix. This would make the empirical case easier to audit.

I also have some concerns about the training data selection strategy. TrialMaster is trained on two randomly selected proofs among the shortest five of ten trial-and-error traces per theorem. This introduces a bias toward shorter traces, and indeed the exploratory study suggests shorter traces work better than longer ones. That is interesting, but it also means the method is not really “learning from the whole proof tree” in the strongest sense suggested earlier in the paper. Rather, it is learning from curated short trial-and-error traces. This is perfectly acceptable, but the paper should be more precise. It would also be useful to know how sensitive performance is to the number of traces per theorem, to trace diversity, and to the ratio of failed to successful steps in training.

On the technical side, some claims need sharper wording. For example, the statement that TrialMaster “can perform backtracking without help from an external system” is only partially true, since Lean is still used to validate each non-backtrack tactic and produce the next state. More importantly, the model is not autonomously maintaining a verified search tree; it is being prompted with the externally maintained history. Similarly, saying the model “outputs the entire proof path after” but only the first tactic is used is confusing and suggests inefficiency or mismatch between training and deployment. Why train/generate full continuations if only the first action matters? An explicit next-action formulation might be cleaner and more comparable to standard tactic prediction.

The writing is generally understandable, but there are many grammatical issues, repetitions, and imprecise statements. Some examples include overclaiming “complete, scalable, and representative,” inconsistent terminology around proof paths versus proof trees, and awkward phrasing in several sections. The tables also appear to have formatting issues in the provided text. The paper would benefit from careful editing for clarity and precision.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has merit. The controlled setting is a strength, not a weakness, as long as the claims are scoped appropriately. The ablation result in Table 3 is substantial and supports the central hypothesis that trial-and-error supervision helps under a matched inference protocol. The dataset could be useful to others studying search-aware training, imitation of proof procedures, or failure-conditioned reasoning. The work also raises an interesting broader question: should theorem-proving models be trained not just on successful proofs but on search processes? That is a worthwhile direction.

To strengthen the paper, I would recommend the following. First, make the matched ablation the centerpiece of the empirical argument, and tone down claims based on the less controlled TrialMaster-versus-DFS comparison. Second, add stronger baselines: same inference format without failure traces, trial-and-error training without explicit backtrack tokens, and perhaps a simple supervised classifier over whether to backtrack. Third, report exact OOD numbers in tables, with confidence intervals over multiple seeds. Fourth, provide more analysis of what is learned: frequency and utility of backtracks, common failure modes, examples where failure-aware training changes the chosen tactic, and whether the model avoids repeating previously failed actions. Fifth, clarify dataset statistics in more detail: provability rate, proof length distributions, trace length distributions, theorem diversity, and the effect of the incompleteness assumption. Sixth, moderate the “representative” language and more carefully discuss limitations of synthetic FPS-generated traces.

My overall assessment is moderately positive. The paper asks a good question, builds a useful controlled benchmark, and presents promising evidence that learning from failed proof attempts can improve theorem proving in intuitionistic propositional logic. However, the current experimental design does not fully isolate the source of gains, and the claims should be narrowed to match the scope of the evidence. With stronger controls and clearer analysis, this could become a solid contribution.

If I were making a conference recommendation, I would lean borderline accept for a venue that values clean empirical studies and benchmark creation, but borderline reject for a highly selective venue unless the authors can better control the comparisons and sharpen the claims. The idea is good; the evidence is encouraging; the paper needs more rigor in attribution and evaluation.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies whether large language models for theorem proving benefit from training on trial-and-error trajectories rather than only successful proof paths. The authors introduce PropL, a Lean-formalized dataset of intuitionistic propositional logic theorems with proofs generated by a focused proof search procedure that records both successful and failed/backtracked steps. They fine-tune Llama-2-7B in two settings: a conventional tactic generator trained only on correct proofs and used within a DFS search procedure, and TrialMaster, trained on proofs containing trial-and-error information and allowed to emit either Lean tactics or explicit backtrack instructions. On their PropL benchmark, especially on a harder split defined by longer proof lengths, TrialMaster reportedly achieves higher success rate and lower Lean-call search cost than the DFS baseline, and an ablation suggests substantial gains from including trial-and-error data.
strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and underexplored mismatch between training on only successful proof traces and inference-time search that necessarily encounters failures and backtracking.
The dataset contribution is potentially useful: PropL is Lean-formalized, automatically checkable, and includes trial-and-error trajectories, which are rare in public theorem-proving resources.
The experimental question is clear and the proposed method is conceptually simple: expose the model to failed branches and backtracking behavior during fine-tuning.
The evaluation includes both success rate and a search-cost proxy (number of Lean calls), which is appropriate for theorem proving systems.
The ablation comparing training with versus without trial-and-error information, while limited, supports the central claim that such information is beneficial in this setting.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow: all experiments are on automatically generated intuitionistic propositional logic theorems, a highly structured and relatively limited domain, so the broader relevance to theorem proving with LLMs is unclear.

The comparison is not fully apples-to-apples because TrialMaster and the DFS baseline use materially different inference procedures, failure criteria, and action spaces; improvements cannot be attributed cleanly to training on failure data alone.

The paper makes strong claims such as the dataset being 'representative' and 'uniformly sampled from all possible theorems,' but these claims are not convincingly justified for the practically used finite, length-constrained distribution.
Important experimental details are missing or underreported, including variance across runs/seeds, exact prompt formats, tokenization/context accounting, and statistical significance.
The baseline set is weak. There is no comparison to stronger search-based or error-aware methods beyond a conventional DFS tactic generator, limiting the significance of the empirical gains.
Results presentation is incomplete in the provided text: key OOD results rely on Figure 5, but the exact full table of success/cost across settings is not clearly reported in the main text.
methodological_flaws: The central causal claim is confounded. TrialMaster differs from the baseline in both training data and inference algorithm: it is trained on trial-and-error traces and also allowed to emit explicit backtrack instructions while conditioning on the full proof tree history. The DFS baseline is trained only on successful traces and searches by sampling multiple tactics per state. Therefore the reported gains do not isolate whether the benefit comes from failure-aware training, a different decoding/search policy, richer conditioning context, or the explicit backtrack action format.

The evaluation protocol is asymmetric. TrialMaster fails immediately on a Lean error, whereas DFS can continue exploring alternatives after invalid tactics at a state because it samples multiple candidates and backtracks externally. Conversely, TrialMaster's backtrack instructions incur no Lean calls, making the search-cost metric structurally favorable to the proposed method. This weakens the fairness of the search-cost comparison.

The proof-generation procedure is intentionally incomplete due to the assumption that once an implication is picked, it cannot be used to show its premise. The paper states this affects about 1 in 1000 provable theorems, but this incompleteness means the dataset and evaluation distribution are induced by the search heuristic rather than the full theorem space, undermining claims of completeness/representativeness.

The claim of 'uniformly sampling from all possible theorems' is scientifically imprecise. Sampling integers uniformly over a finite range and mapping them bijectively to formulas of fixed size does not imply a natural or theorem-relevant uniform distribution over provable propositions, and the subsequent filtering/splitting by proof lengths further distorts the distribution.

The train/test split may still permit substantial structural overlap because all formulas have the same number of internal nodes and are generated from the same grammar and proof procedure; separating by proof length quantiles is not a strong guarantee of out-of-distribution generalization.

The ablation in Table 3 is also not fully controlled: the model trained without trial-and-error is evaluated using the TrialMaster-style one-step greedy inference, which may be poorly matched to its training objective. This makes the large gap difficult to interpret purely as evidence for the value of failure data.

The statement that all generated backtracking instructions point to existing states is not sufficient evidence that the model learned semantically correct backtracking; format validity is weaker than demonstrating that backtracking decisions improve search in a controlled analysis.
There is no statistical uncertainty analysis. With 1000-example test sets, differences such as 88.7% vs 88.4% may not be meaningful without confidence intervals or repeated runs.
